newsitem.title: USA: Nazis sold Holocaust victims' gold to Swiss - report.
newsitem.headline: Nazis sold Holocaust victims' gold to Swiss - report.

text.p: A long-awaited U.S. government report will state there is conclusive evidence that the Nazis sold Switzerland gold stolen from individual Holocaust victims, sources close to the State Department said on Friday.
The sources said the 11-agency report will also show that after the war, Switzerland failed to return billions of dollars worth of looted Nazi gold it received during World War Two.
The more than 200-page report, based on 14 million pages of U.S. government documents, was prepared under the direction of Under Secretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat.
It is expected to be released next Wednesday, and the sources said it will be extremely harsh on the Swiss role in the war as bankers and even money-launderers for the Third Reich.

The report, however, will not make any recommendations as to whether the United States should reopen a 1946 treaty with Switzerland in which the Swiss agreed to return $58 million of the Nazi gold received during the war.
Documents in the report will show that the Swiss took in $425 million in looted gold -- worth more than $4.25 billion a current prices.

Sources who have read the report told Reuters it will contain proof that Germany not only sent Switzerland gold stolen from the national treasuries of the countries it occupied, but also gold taken by the Nazi SS as loot from individual victims.

In Zurich, a spokesman for the Swiss National Bank (SNB), which acknowledges buying nearly 250 tonnes of the some 336 tonnes of gold Germany sent to Switzerland during the war, would not confirm Swiss purchases of Holocaust victims' gold.

"We have never found any evidence in our own files here in Switzerland that gold from private sources, notably from the concentration camps, was among the gold sold to the Swiss National Bank," spokesman Werner Abegg said.

"The Allied gold warnings of 1943 and 1944 that warned neutral countries not to accept gold from Germany never in any way mentioned or even alluded to the possibility that gold from private sources or even from the concentration camps could be in the shipments from Germany," he added.
But he added historians examining Switzerland's World War Two role as a financial centre would have to delve into this.
SNB Chairman Hans Meyer said last month that around two-thirds of the gold Nazi Germany sent to Switzerland came from official reserves seized from occupied countries.
He did not say where the other third came from, but was apparently referring to Germany's own holdings.
The German SS looted personal jewelry, watches, rings and even the gold dental fillings of their victims, many of them Jews herded into notorious death camps such as Auschwitz.
The camp gold was then sent to German central bank where it was resmelted, U.S. archival documents said.
The sources told Reuters that investigators had found the smelting records of gold sold to Switzerland by the Nazis and it showed conclusively that victim gold was mixed with bank gold.
Documents to be appended to the report show that after the war, Switzerland returned to the Allies only about 15 percent of the looted gold it bought from Germany.

Sources close to the U.S. State Department said other documents showed that victim gold wound up in the gold pool of a commission set up by the Allies after the war to return the looted metal to its rightful owners.
The Allied-established Tripartite Gold Commission also has long maintained that all the captured Nazi gold in its holdings were from the banks of Europe and none came from individuals.
The distinction is important because all of the $4 billion worth of gold it has distributed went to central banks and not one ounce went to Holocaust survivors.
The commission distributed all but 5.5 tonnes of some 377 tonnes it received from Britain, France and the United States.

Abegg said the SNB considered the 1946 treaty on gold transactions between Switzerland and Germany final and added it was up to the Allies to determine why individuals were not compensated for gold stolen by the Nazis.
"It is essentially the work of the Allies or maybe the U.S. to clarify that point," he said.
